speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head U of the Estimates be reduced by $100." The tragedy of climate change is not that it is not severe or insignificant.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The real tragedy is that few people think of it urgently and deeply.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have been speaking in the past about how Singapore has, over time, built up its water security as well as various measures to reduce our weight on the environment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A few years ago, we set up the Singapore Centre for Climate Research in 2013.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are a member of the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Last year, we put in place a carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But climate change requires all of us across different departments and Ministries to work together.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given our long memories of floods, we have pump houses that transport storm water from reservoirs to the sea.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our beautiful Marina Barrage is actually a glorified anti-flooding pump.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Meanwhile, we have seen one of the largest players in Singapore's built environment, that is, the Housing and Development Board (HDB), making a big difference under the Greenprint programme, where solar panels and waste conveyance systems are embedded or will be embedded into HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On roads, there is now a determined push into more and better public transport systems – new service lines, larger bus fleets and bike-sharing initiatives.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the way we live, move and make money, Singapore is turning green.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We started life as a nation as a Garden City as a way to distinguish ourselves as a disciplined and well-ordered society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, it goes without saying that we need a whole-of-nation effort to deal with climate change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How is our Government working to foster collective action by businesses, the community and individuals to tackle this issue together?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, we have heard much about Singapore's commitment to climate change and this is, indeed, encouraging.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There was a consultation exercise on our long-term low-emissions development strategy last year.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean share what is the outcome of this?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Could Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean also share if we are on track to meet our commitment to the Paris Agreement?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As we transit to a low-carbon future, what is the expected impact on our economy?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will it add to the cost of doing business in Singapore and, therefore, drive away some investors?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On the other hand, how is Singapore leveraging green growth opportunities?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, I am gratified that Singapore has always been conscious of the drastic impact that climate change has on our generation and, more importantly, on future generations.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am in support of the bold and proactive steps that the Government has taken over the last few years to reduce our carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Given that there are limited alternative renewable sources viable in Singapore, I would like to ask the Minister how Singapore will further reduce the emission from our energy consumption.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As Singapore builds, a proposal would be to consider the entire lifecycle of building materials and choose to use materials that can be recycled or reused, such as, for drains and roads.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It would also be in our future vision to build and convert existing buildings to zero-energy or net-zero energy buildings.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a whole country effort is required to reduce emissions, I would also ask the Minister if we can create a National Green Mark to recognise local projects and businesses with initiatives and practices which reduce emissions and grant incentives to the finance sector to provide funding to such businesses and projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Climate change is a substantial threat to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Not only must we protect our shores from rising waters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must also fulfil our international obligations towards low carbon emissions development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We cannot survive on a moral island burning fossil fuels while the rest of the world struggles to keep the cities above rising waters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The core to this must be a national strategy and blueprint that guide our agencies and people preparing for the city's future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, the journey to protect ourselves is fraught with dilemmas and tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Controlling carbon emission through carbon taxes increases business costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Protecting our coastlines might have permanent ecological impact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How are the key stakeholders, such as businesses, green groups and academics, consulted?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must develop a strategy that balances tradeoffs and brings together generations of people to pursue our climate change objectives sustainably.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This meant that inter-generational tradeoffs must be balanced carefully.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As we have turned water scarcity into valuable knowledge of market value, what are the strategies that we pursuing to turn these threats into opportunities?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The severity and enormity of the challenge require us to plan way ahead but execute quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the concrete plans and programmes that have already been put in place since the Prime Minister’s announcement during the last National Day Rally?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would also significantly enlarge our green footprint and boost our contribution to reduce the debilitating effects of climate change.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, on the prospects of a pan-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) electricity grid, an SP official was quoted as saying that Malaysia already has connections to Thailand which, in turn, has connections to Laos.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Hypothetically, therefore, Singapore could invest in clean energy projects in neighbouring countries beyond our immediate neighbours and use renewable energy credits to receive the same amount of electricity from Malaysia, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What does this mean for the consumer and power generators in Singapore, not to mention the price of electricity?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand some discussions have already taken place with Malaysia for greater cooperation in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What risk does the Government anticipate in reducing our carbon footprint by diversifying and tapping on regional electricity grids and how can these be overcome?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of easier access to the markets and our research and development (R&D) sector, how can Singapore contribute to addressing regional climate change challenges and imagining commercial solutions in view of the active interest in addressing climate change, a top policy priority for younger Singaporeans in particular?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Temperatures around the world continue to rise, melting ice into oceans and causing sea levels to rise.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This poses existential challenges to our island state.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We have to act decisively on climate change.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am heartened that the Government has carried out a public consultation in 2019 to discuss how we could formulate our long-term low-emissions development strategy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Government share its plans to reduce our emissions?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What are the various factors the Government took into consideration?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Moving ahead, we also need to look into achieving sustainable development, continue to create good jobs while ensuring a well-managed transition to a low-carbon future.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The transition, while challenging, also poses various opportunities in the green economy-related innovation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How can Singapore leverage green growth opportunities and how we plan to rally businesses, the community and individuals to be part of it?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, climate change is a global issue that requires collective efforts on a united and international front.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond mitigating our domestic emissions, how can Singapore contribute to international efforts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the key areas of international cooperation needed to achieve Singapore's climate goals?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have, in a Parliamentary Question before, expressed my concerns on our role in Coal-fired and Gas-fired Independent Power Producer (IPP) Projects in the ASEAN region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Senior Minister also share how they have been supporting our financial sector to make the transition to promote more green financing in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope we can explore my proposal to kickstart a first loss fund for renewables projects in ASEAN, with other ASEAN sovereign wealth funds, including Singapore's, chipping in later on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is certainly something I have discussed on other occasions at various forums for investors and financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But for the Singapore Government, in this case, to spearhead the efforts, will be a very good opportunity to boost our international profile and it will be a more effective way for ASEAN and Singapore to reduce carbon emissions globally, more effectively and fast.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chairman, the Government's commitment to a low carbon future and reduction of greenhouse gases is welcomed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I understand that the Young People's Action Party (PAP) conducted a focus group discussion recently with climate activists and experts from the sustainability sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Amongst the issues discussed was the perceived over-emphasis on economic metrics as a means of calculating growth.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some felt that such metrics encouraged excessive production and consumption.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Also, the current calculations of emission levels against GDP value may not truly reflect current performance levels.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Can the Government give an update on Singapore's plans moving forward?

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, across the globe, the effects of climate change are clear and present.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Weather patterns have become more extreme; ice sheets and glaciers are melting.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore, too, has experienced more episodes of unusually heavy rainfall accompanied by some flooding.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Prolonged dry weather exacerbates the smoke haze that affects our region.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As a low-lying island, we remain fundamentally vulnerable.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change (IMCCC), which I chair, was formed in 2007.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: IMCCC coordinates, formulates and monitors the execution of our national plans to reduce our carbon emissions, referred to as mitigation, and to prepare for the consequences of climate change, referred to as adaptation.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In his Budget speech, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat stated Singapore's intention to chart our vision for a low-carbon, sustainable future.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Allow me, Mr Chairman, to inform this House of our plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our enhanced 2030 NDC and LEDS build on policies and initiatives we have progressively implemented over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They demonstrate our seriousness and commitment to support international climate action and a low-carbon future.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Setting out our vision well in advance will provide a clear sense of direction and give ourselves and our various stakeholders the time to effect a well-managed transition to a low-carbon economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This will also allow us to grow new sectors in our economy and create new jobs and opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Ong Teng Koon and Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked about the Government's approach and strategies for climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The development of our enhanced NDC for 2030 and our LEDS aspiration for 2050 and beyond, is guided by a principled approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is considered, it is committed and it is collective.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We fully appreciate the significance and impact of climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is why climate change policy is being strongly coordinated as a key whole-of-nation issue under PMO.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our climate policies and strategies are carefully and thoroughly considered.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At the same time, we are not exclusively focused on climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We look at realistic and practical policies and measures we can implement, taking into account the best available science and technology, and fully integrated with the larger context of the entire range of challenges we face in our national policy framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is the approach we take to ensure a smooth and well-managed transition to a low-carbon economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have always believed that the pursuit of economic growth can be compatible and mutually reinforcing with environmental objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This approach has allowed Singapore today to have one of the lowest carbon emissions per GDP dollar, or emissions intensity.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are ranked among the 20 best countries out of 141 countries in 2017.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our performance on the Human Development Index and the UN Sustainable Development Goals are also very commendable.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We invited views and consulted Singaporeans on important climate issues, such as the carbon tax, achieving zero waste and our LEDS.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We received many suggestions on how to reduce our emissions, in fact, over 2,000.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At the same time, our contributors also recognised that there are practical constraints and potential tradeoffs.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In particular, we are very mindful of our limited alternative energy options.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore's geography is a key limiting factor in our ability to harness renewable energy at scale.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We do not have great rivers for hydropower.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Wind power is limited both by space as well as light and variable winds.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We continue to study the potential for nuclear power, but we assess that the current generation of nuclear power plants are not suitable for deployment in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, these are serious constraints compared to better-endowed countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Nevertheless, we are committed to doing our best and doing our part to combat climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our enhanced NDC and LEDS set out realistic but challenging and ambitious goals for Singapore, drawing on citizens' suggestions and taking into account our national circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are on track to meet this commitment.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Constraining our total emissions within this absolute cap up to 2030 means that every sector in Singapore will need to put in significant efforts to limit our emissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will need to do so in order to move towards a low carbon nation in the coming decade, with new commercial and industrial enterprises and new growth areas, such as the digital economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We all have a part to play in reducing our emissions to meet our 2030 commitment.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But we aim to do better than that beyond 2030.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And with your permission, Mr Chairman, may I display a slide on the House's screens and request the Clerks to distribute a document to Members?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this will help take us from the left-hand side, where we have our 2030 NDC through these three thrusts to the right-hand side, which is our LEDS for 2050 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Each thrust will contribute to halving our emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will pursue all three vigorously to achieve our aspiration.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The extent to which potential emission reductions from each thrust can be realised will become clearer in the coming years, as we gain experience from implementing our programmes, as technology evolves and as the modalities for international cooperation and collaboration become formalised.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If the actual reductions from each thrust are larger than we now assess, or are available sooner, then we can realise our aspiration earlier.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On the other hand, if the potential reductions turn out to be less promising, we will still strive to meet our LEDS aspiration to the best of our ability even though the task becomes more difficult.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, let me now provide some details of the various programmes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Keeping carbon emissions low from electrical power generation, which currently accounts for 39% of our emissions – that is the yellow sector on the right.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is very important, especially as we push for greater electrification of our nation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In October 2019, Minister Chan Chun Sing outlined how we will harness the four supply switches of "natural gas”, "solar", "regional power grids and "low carbon alternatives", together with greater efficiency in energy use on the demand side to accelerate our energy transformation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To achieve our current goal by the end of this year of 350 MWp, we are deploying solar panels on about one in two HDB rooftops, and in several reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To achieve two GWp, we will do more.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are deploying offshore solar farms, and HDB aims to install as many solar panels as feasible on HDB rooftops.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As an example, in Pasir Ris town, almost all HDB rooftops will have solar panels by 2030 and deployment is already progressing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Minister for National Development Lawrence Wong will say more about greening our towns in the Ministry of National Development's (MND's) COS debate.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Even at such a scale, two GWp of solar power will still only meet around 4% of our current annual electricity needs and 10% of our current peak daily electricity needs.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To go significantly beyond this, we need technical breakthroughs, for example, to deploy safe and highly-efficient and cost-effective solar panels on vertical building surfaces, not just horizontal ones.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These building surfaces will only receive solar radiation for part of the day.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this is why we still need the other three switches to decarbonise our grid.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To provide our base load power generation, we had decided early on, in the early 2000s, to switch from fuel oil to natural gas, the cleanest fossil fuel available.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Many countries are still highly dependent on coal.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We moved away from that in 1956 and we moved to natural gas in the early 2000s.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are exploring tapping regional power grids and studying emerging low or zero-carbon alternatives, such as solar-derived hydrogen to further reduce emissions from power generation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Having regional power grids is an alternative, but we also have to examine the issues of diversity and resilience.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have diversified the way for piped water and piped natural gas.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We should also have diversity when we are considering piped electricity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For industries with sizeable electricity consumption, the progressive decarbonisation of our power grid will help to reduce emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we will also need to reduce emissions all across our economy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The industry sector, at 60%, is our largest contributor to carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will work closely with the industry to make the necessary adjustments, capture new business opportunities and build up their competitive advantage in this transition.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We want to be at the forefront of the global move towards environmentally sustainable production and seize the new opportunities this creates.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Our industries produce not just for Singapore but also to meet the needs of the global market.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will work with our industries so that they are known to be among the best-in-class in global energy and carbon efficiency as we produce for the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Last year, we enhanced our grant schemes to help companies improve their energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are also going beyond individual companies to bring companies together to achieve systems-level efficiency gains.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are also working with industry and our research community to study new technologies, such as CCUS and low-carbon hydrogen, to evaluate and plan the next steps for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We intend to invest more than that into helping our companies adapt, move and transform for a low-carbon future.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In urban transportation, we are already a global pioneer in limiting vehicle population and reducing traffic congestion.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These policies tackle the urban transport issue systemically, not just individual pieces of it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is where most of the gains in energy and carbon efficiency are reaped.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we will also move towards enhancing the overall carbon efficiency of our urban transport through large-scale adoption of green vehicles.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources (MEWR) and MND will say more about how we will provide incentives and lay the enabling charging infrastructure to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These efforts will make a significant difference, but how quickly they can be realised depends on technological advancements and how quickly manufacturers can bring attractive, cost-efficient electric vehicles (EVs) to the market.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Our commercial and residential buildings are also major users of energy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Since the launch of the Green Mark Scheme in 2005, we have greened more than 40% of our buildings by gross floor area.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will push on to achieve our goal to green 80% of our buildings by 2030 and beyond that, we aim to increase the number of buildings that are even more energy-efficient.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: All of us have a part to play.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have introduced minimum energy performance standards (MEPS) and mandatory energy labelling (MELS) for common household appliances.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: By purchasing more efficient appliances, consumers save on their energy costs while reducing emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Just by this step alone, we can save money and reduce carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui, Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how Singapore is contributing to international efforts on climate change.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Singapore will do our utmost to work with the international community to tackle climate change.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Every country must do its part or the efforts of each country will be nullified.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Singapore works actively in international forums to strengthen consensus among countries, especially at a time when the multilateral system is under strain.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Singapore is often called upon as a constructive and trusted interlocutor to help forge solutions for difficult issues at international climate negotiations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For example, Minister Masagos Zulkifli played key roles in co-facilitating the topic of mitigation at COP-24 in Katowice in 2018 and the key outcomes of the climate negotiations in Madrid last December.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We look forward to working closely with the United Kingdom, which will be hosting COP-26 in Glasgow this November.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are also well-positioned to support abatement efforts globally.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As a major maritime and aviation hub, we work actively with the International Maritime Organization and International Civil Aviation Organization to address international transport emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Ministry of Transport will share more details later.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As a leading financial centre, we aim to be a green finance hub to spur investments in low-carbon solutions and drive climate action.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: MAS also collaborated with the industry to develop environmental risk management guidelines.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These guidelines will set standards on governance, risk management and disclosure, and encourage the right-pricing of loans and investments to promote new green investments.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: MAS will issue the guidelines for public consultation in March 2020.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think Mr Saktiandi Supaat will be happy to know that our three local banks have stopped funding regional coal-fired power plant projects and all three of them are very active in financing regional alternative energy projects, such as solar power.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Through our Research Innovation and Enterprise 2020 plan, we are investing close to $1 billion in urban solutions and sustainability in areas, such as new urban mobility solutions and a next-generation energy grid.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As a "living lab", we will continue to serve as a testbed for innovative solutions that can be exported globally.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Singapore also collaborates actively with international partners, such as the UNFCCC and ASEAN, to build capabilities and share experiences.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Since 1992, Singapore has trained more than 130,000 officials from fellow developing countries under the Singapore Cooperation Programme (SCP) in key areas, such as sustainable development, urban planning, water and transport management.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: While Singapore's efforts to reduce emissions on our own may be modest, our collective efforts with all nations can be substantial.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Chairman, for small-island nations like Singapore, climate change poses an asymmetrical challenge.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We need to implement these adaptation plans to protect our country and people, and we cannot rely on anyone else to do this for us.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The highest tide ever recorded in Singapore is about two metres above SHD.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Raising the level from three metres to four metres gives us an additional one metre of clearance and gives us a two-metre buffer, so that if sea levels rise by one metre, we still have one metre left.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Marina Barrage, which was completed in 2008, already provides some flood protection for our city, but we are planning to see whether we can raise that further and even increase the size of the pumps.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Protecting ourselves from sea level rise is a large-scale and long-term effort requiring considerable resources.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Our assessments and plans are based on studies which have been commissioned by the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change over the past several years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will now develop these studies into detailed plans and phases in our coastal protection measures.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We must start implementing our plans and be prepared to adjust and adapt them according to the latest sea level rise projections.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources will say more about this in the debate in his COS.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I have just outlined our whole-of-Government strategy for climate action, which is considered, committed and collective.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The relevant Ministries will provide more details on specific plans under their charge.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But as Mr Seah Kian Peng has highlighted, this is a collective effort.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We need all Singaporeans – the Government, individuals, households and businesses – all of us, to do our part and work together as a whole of nation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As part of Singapore Together, the Government will create more partnership opportunities for Singaporeans to advance climate action.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, let us work together to secure the future of Singapore as a climate-resilient nation, with a competitive economy, sustainable environment, an environmentally responsible and active citizenry, and a good quality of life for all.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is a 1.2% increase from the previous year.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The number of Singapore Citizens is 3.5 million and the number of Permanent Residents (PRs) is 525,000.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is a slight increase of 0.8% and 0.6% respectively.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It means that we only have 4.5 residents who are between the age of 20 and 64 for every resident who is 65 and above.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the Government doing to increase or at least to maintain our Singapore Citizens' numbers?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can we do more to support young families and encourage more Singaporean families to have more babies?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the Government doing to slow down the increase of old-age support ratio?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Immigration has for a very long time been a touchy issue, not only in Singapore but many other countries as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Generally, most Singaporeans accept that immigration can contribute certain expertise that is lacking in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many of them chose to make Singapore their home and become citizens.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They take their pledge at citizenship ceremonies that are held across different constituencies.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: A survey by the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) released at the National Integration Council (NIC) Convention last August showed that many Singaporeans feel that immigrants can do more to integrate into Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This survey covered about 4,000 Singapore Citizens and PRs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Six out of 10 of the respondents felt that the immigrants were not doing enough to integrate.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is there any study or survey on our new citizens on how they feel about their new citizenship journey?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Do they feel adequately integrated by our programmes?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can we do more to make them be more integrated?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the Government doing to further enhance the integration of new citizens into our society and our communities?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: While the Finance Minister's Budget speeches in this term of Government focused consistently on security, economy, society and Singaporeans, we know that our evolving population policies are existential to the future of the Singapore Core.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The same document, however, records an encouraging rise in the TFR for the Malay community.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Has the PMO team assessed the policy reasons behind this upturn for the Malay community and are there insights that can be highlighted or even ported over to the other communities?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Similarly, the latest data also records a rise in the number of citizen ever married females deciding to have no children, or only one child compared to 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Likewise, the proportion of married females with three children or more has fallen considerably over the same period.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Fortunately, most ever married citizen females who have two children has hovered around the 43% mark, similar to 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: While the decision to have children or no children is a deeply personal one and one that we must respect, what new strategies and plans does PMO have to push couples or encourage couples to have at least two or more children?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Has the Government engaged couples who have only one child to find out what their key concerns are?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I believe work-life balance, costs of living concerns have been raised previously as major impediments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It would be important to see what more can be done in this area with buy-in from private sector employers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: After all, without a thriving Singapore Core, it is hard to foresee a thriving and confident Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Numbers aside, the Government needs to take a relook at our integration efforts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: PRs and foreigners who we hope will take up citizenship are connected through technology to their motherlands more so than earlier generations of immigrants.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Therefore, integration may not just take more time, but may not be as linear as previously imagined with schools and institutions, such as National Service, our major agents of adhesion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In addition, as alluded to by Minister Chan Chun Sing recently, unlike in the past, even in the economic realm, Singapore may not be able to attract the quality of individuals it seeks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What shifts in our population strategies is the Government planning so as to deal with the new challenges in supplementing our population through immigration?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Has the Government conducted surveys of new citizens over the last 10 to 20 years, for us to have a better perspective on how we can improve integration?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What are the their main reasons for not transiting to citizenship?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She is our fourth child and our first daughter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Having lost two of our six children, Peter and Maria, to miscarriages, every time we go through a pregnancy, we have an equal measure of worry and joy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Each time our gynaecologist says, "She’s doing fine", we let out a sigh of relief.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Clare's birth has changed our lives, just as her three older brothers have.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The home is a little bit noisier, the floor is, of course, a lot messier and sleep is now even more a luxury commodity at home, but, more importantly, the immeasurable joy of parenthood.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Like everything else, it comes with its own burdens.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But Jocelyn and I believe that it is a burden worth carrying.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same time, I wish the burden were lighter, not so much with benefits, but for society to be able to reinforce a culture that recognises the family as important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For our three older boys, she took care of them herself without any help.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And often, I am asked, "What does your wife work as"?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My reply that she is a full-time mother often elicits odd responses.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They go along the lines of, "Oh, she is so lucky, she doesn't have to work", or on the flipside, "You have to work harder." Often enough, I respond quite quickly to those statements, as if to justify our situation; that in addition to her love for our children, she also runs a small online business at home that twins her passions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it also hits me after that that there is no need to justify why my wife stays at home.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She, like other stay-at-home mothers, make a conscious decision, that a sacrifice of her career was weighed and that spending time with the children was worth it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A fellow parliamentarian from Europe, whom I have known for a few years, was in Singapore for a conference last year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He made an observation, perhaps a little snidely and a little bit snarky, "The Minister-in-charge of your country's population strategy is the Minister for Manpower?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Should it not be the Minister for Family?" I explained to him that our Minister-in-charge only happens to be the Minister for Manpower.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She is also a mother, and also a Cabinet Minister who is deeply passionate about children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But there might be a small grain of truth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Often, we couch our policies on families with the view on our workforce, our dependency ratio, so much so that our culture has been shaped by that; that the true joy and happiness of family are clouded by numbers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, I urge, as I have in the last three years, for us a return to basics, that we ask ourselves beyond policies, beyond benefits, how can the whole of society help to build a family-friendly culture that is supportive of families in Singapore, that allows stay-at-home mothers to be proud of what they do?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And also for mothers who choose to continue their careers to have the support that they require.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That said, I also wish that we level the playing field and recognise fully the role of mothers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, families are the backbone of society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we do not take care of this backbone, we will not be able to stand straight and strong as a country.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Marriage and parenthood can be a joyful journey.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, there are challenges, but the joy of bringing up children is fulfilling and lasting.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, the Government conducted public consultations on the needs and concerns relevant to marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And will there be further enhancements based on feedback received?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Younger Singaporeans may be delaying marriage and parenthood in pursuit of other life goals.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, how can the whole-of-society contribute to building a culture that emphasises the importance and significance of family and, in so doing, foster an environment that is supportive of families in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will help also to promote the desire to have children – a joy for the parents and also, importantly, for our country.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How have the enhancements benefited young Singaporeans and what was their feedback, especially from the Citizens Panel?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Core to singles not getting married and married couples not having children is the intricate balance between work and family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Having FWAs can help our families cope better, especially after maternity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Coronavirus Disease of 2019 (COVID-19) episode has shown that broad-based FWA is possible whereas the previous pre-outbreak thinking was that it simply was not.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Government consider granting women on maternity the right to FWA?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will PMO consider having specific childcare sick leave and providing this on a per child basis?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government clearly feels that childcare sick leave is important for people who work for us, then why is it not important for the people we serve?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many of us spend a large part of our day and, in fact, our lives at work.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is, therefore, important for both our mental and physical well-being that there is a healthy culture in the workplace environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Social norms and the workplace culture can impact Singaporeans' decisions on important issues like marriage, having children and career progression.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of the key challenges faced by parents with young children is managing their work and family responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If they find this too challenging, they may not want to have more children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, we must also ensure that those who are single at the workplace are not the ones having to pick up the workload of their colleagues who have children, because this may prevent them from having opportunities to have relationships and eventually marry.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It was indicated that the Government would seriously study the recommendations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How will the Government be following up on the Panel's recommendations, and how can employers and other stakeholders play a bigger role in implementing solutions to make workplaces more family-friendly?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Citizens Panel was convened to gather views from Singaporeans from all walks of life on how work-life harmony can be strengthened in Singapore and how a more supportive society-workplace culture can be created that is family-friendly.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that youths will shape the future workplace culture of Singapore, what has been the feedback from youths from the Citizens' Panel on how they see work-life balance?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Have they shared how they can balance pursuing their aspirations with starting a family and how they see society supporting them in achieving this balance?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In recent conversations with youths, some have shared their interest to work and study overseas.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government is also promoting this, so that youths have a wider perspective and can also gain international experience which is extremely helpful in their careers and personal development.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do youths reconcile the internationalisation message with settling down with a family in Singapore?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I appreciate the views and suggestions of Members on matters concerning our population.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our policies aim to help Singapore maintain a stable population, to keep our society cohesive, our economy vibrant, and our nation strong.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Population policies are not just for today, but tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are always thinking about future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will focus on two areas: first, making Singapore a great place for families; second, integrating immigrants into our Singapore community.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We aim, first and foremost, to support young Singaporeans to get married and become parents.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Globally, many countries are like Singapore, where birth rates have been declining since the 1970s.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some Nordic countries that had previously reversed the decline, have seen birth rates falling again in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, there are some positive signs in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The average number of citizen births in the last five years is higher than previous five-year periods.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I believe Mr Alex Yam, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Louis Ng, Ms Rahayu Mahzam and also Ms Sun Xueling, perhaps Mr Pritam Singh as well, all contributed to this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is also higher than the average in previous five-year periods.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, to Ms Sun Xueling's question, it is not incompatible – your overseas ambitions and raising a family – this can be done.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I hope these positive trends will continue as more young Singaporeans enter their prime marriage and parenthood ages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we will need to continue tackling the factors that shape marriage and parenthood decisions together, not just as a Government, but as one Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the Committee of Supply debate last year, I indicated that we would embark on a consultation process to better understand Singaporeans’ needs and concerns around forming families.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The aim was to move beyond feedback and suggestions to work with fellow Singaporeans on practical ways to address marriage and parenthood issues.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is what the Singapore Together movement is all about.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are heartened that many Singaporeans stepped forward to take part.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We launched a series of online polls, inviting Singaporeans to give suggestions on how to better support young families.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza and Ms Sun Xueling mentioned, Singaporeans believe that making Singapore a great place for families requires partnerships across society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At home, most Singaporeans viewed parenting as a shared responsibility between spouses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the workplace, Singaporeans felt that having supportive bosses and understanding colleagues were critical factors that enabled them to meet their work and family commitments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Respondents also raised concerns about the cost of having children.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, we announced significant enhancements to support young families.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Desmond Choo asked how these enhancements have benefited young Singaporean families.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, couples can now more easily enrol their child in an affordable and good quality preschool.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have increased the amount of preschool subsidies, and made them available to even more families.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is about a third of what they would have paid previously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To ensure that quality preschools are accessible to all families, we have kept fees affordable at all Government-supported preschools.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Fee caps for Partner Operator preschools will also come down next year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) has been growing the number of preschool places.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the medium term, we aim to make full-day childcare at Government-supported preschools as affordable as the cost of primary school plus afterschool student care.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is not even including the means-tested preschool subsidies, which will allow low- and middle-income families to pay even less.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, we will ensure good quality learning and care across all preschools.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are significant steps that we are taking to ensure that we continue to give every Singaporean child a good start in life.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, housing is now more affordable for newly married couples.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have heard couples’ feedback on the importance of getting their own home before starting a family.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have made it faster for them to get a Build-To-Order (BTO) flat.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: HDB has launched more than 3,600 BTO flats with shorter waiting times.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The wait of about two and a half years is shorter than the usual three to four years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Couples can also more easily own a flat with the Enhanced Central Provident Fund (CPF) Housing Grant (EHG).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More couples are able to purchase subsidised HDB flats and Executive Condominiums.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, we improved the affordability of healthcare for children and fertility treatments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By the end of this year, every Singaporean child will enjoy subsidies for all nationally recommended childhood vaccinations and developmental screenings at polyclinics as well as Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) general practitioner (GP) clinics.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Minister for Health will share more details at the Ministry of Health's (MOH's) Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also enhanced Government co-funding for assisted conception procedures to better support couples who need them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These enhancements reinforce our strong support for marriage and parenthood in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They have also been well-received by many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam was concerned that many Singaporeans find it a challenge to balance work and family.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked whether there would be further enhancements based on feedback received.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have been working on ways to help families achieve better harmony in work and life, including whether to have longer leave for parents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At present, working couples have a combined total of 20 weeks of paid parental leave and two weeks of unpaid leave in their child’s first year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, each parent receives six days of paid childcare leave annually until their child turns seven, and two days of paid childcare leave until the child turns 12.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We announced the three-year Public Sector pilot on Unpaid Infant Care Leave in 2017.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The pilot enables public officers to take up to four weeks of Unpaid Infant Care Leave in the first year after their child’s birth.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This benefit has been well-received by parents who need it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Their supervisors and colleagues have also been supportive and feel that it has not affected their teams’ productivity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We hope that more private companies will be encouraged by the Public Service’s positive experience, and initiate similar support to their employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There have been calls from time to time, including from Mr Louis Ng, to further enhance leave schemes for parents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will continuously review all support measures for parenthood.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We had prioritised housing, preschool and healthcare because these were what young families said mattered most.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Of course, when conditions allow, young families would welcome more paid leave being mandated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, it would be unwise for us to ignore the impact on employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While the public sector is in a position to do more than current legislation requires, we cannot assume the same for all businesses, especially small and medium enterprises (SMEs), which are the single largest group of employers and already facing manpower constraints.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the face of economic uncertainties and the pressure for businesses to transform, the tripartite partners are also mindful not to add further to employers' burdens.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead of imposing higher obligations on all, we will provide greater support to businesses that are able to do more, such as supporting them in implementing FWAs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After all, working parents have consistently given us feedback that FWAs are key in supporting them to manage work and family commitments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I should add that when companies implement FWAs, other employees who are not parents also benefit.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They tend to feel a greater sense of fairness.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, if some do not have young children but have elderly parents who, from time to time, have medical appointments that they also need to take them to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As it turns out, a focus on promoting FWAs was also the preference of the Citizens’ Panel convened last year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Panel brought together 55 fellow Singaporeans of diverse backgrounds to develop ways to improve work-life harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I was heartened by their enthusiasm and commitment to build a future Singapore that would be more supportive of work-life harmony.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Panel recommended thoughtful solutions, such as promoting FWAs and introducing more progressive HR practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These would help employees, especially those with more caregiving responsibilities, to better juggle their family life and work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sun Xueling and Mr Desmond Choo will be glad to know that both younger and older Singaporeans in the Panel called for wider societal change to address social norms that affect work-life harmony and for shifts in workplace practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will introduce new tools and guides to facilitate the adoption of FWAs and work-life harmony initiatives by employers and employees. "Making It Known".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will increase the recognition of employers who adopt FWAs and work-life initiatives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Low Yen Ling will provide more details on these moves at MOM's Committee of Supply debate. "Making It Accepted".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will work together to shift societal norms and the mindsets of employers, employees and individuals in the larger community.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope these efforts will rally Singaporeans to work together, towards a more family-friendly society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Supporting marriage and parenthood is the Government's top priority for the population.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our policies and enhancements over the years attest to that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, I agree with Mr Alex Yam that beyond policy, a whole-of-society approach is needed to build a family-friendly Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For instance, when we see parents with young children struggling with their prams in public spaces, do we step forward to lend a helping hand?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When a colleague goes on paternity leave, do we say supportive words of encouragement or do we cast aspersions on this necessity?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Quite often, it is societal values, workplace and cultural norms that determine whether raising a family is achievable, enjoyable and celebrated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a delicate issue in many places around the world.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With current birth rates and as our society ages, our citizen population will likely decline.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For many years now, we have taken in a carefully controlled number of new citizens each year to keep the citizen population stable over the long term.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As immigrants are mostly from younger age groups, this also helps to moderate our pace of ageing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government has kept the pace of immigration calibrated, in line with our commitments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not easy to become a new citizen or PR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have high expectations of those who join our community.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Newcomers who want to make Singapore their home have the responsibility to adapt to our way of life, and must continue to contribute to our society and economy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One good example is Mr Trieu Dang Huy, who works as a senior projects executive at Singapore Airlines.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He has lived in Singapore for 14 years and became a Singapore Citizen last year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When Mr Trieu first moved here, he took it upon himself to learn English, Mandarin and Singlish, so much so that when he speaks now, it is hard to tell that he was originally from Vietnam.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Trieu met his wife while studying at the National University of Singapore (NUS).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Together, they believe it is important to contribute to society and donate blood regularly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They also have a young son who is Singaporean.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members of this House would know of other examples.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked how we can ensure that newcomers make an effort to integrate into our society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The National Integration Council is doing a lot of commendable work on this front in the community, workplaces and schools.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As part of the Singapore Together movement, we are inviting Singaporeans to help craft the content for the Singapore Citizenship Journey – a compulsory programme for all who seek to take up Singapore citizenship.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, the People's Association appoints Integration and Naturalisation Champions to help new citizens and PRs settle into their neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They organise chit-chat sessions, interest groups and learning journeys to nudge newcomers to make new friends and get involved in the community.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We continue to welcome Singaporeans' views on how we help newcomers to better integrate into our society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As we start the new decade, the Government remains committed to working with Singaporeans and to keep Singaporeans at the heart of our population policies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked for an update on our population outlook.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Mr Chairman, my cut is to ask about the tangible benefits to citizens and local businesses arising from our Smart Nation initiatives.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Digitalisation has opened up new possibilities for businesses and for our society.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But the prestige of being a globally recognised as a "smart city" is scant success if our citizens and businesses are unable to reap tangible benefits.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Can the Minister share with us how our Smart Nation initiatives have created an efficient and competitive environment for our businesses?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Can the Minister also share with us how our Smart Nation policies have engendered inclusiveness and improved the convenience and quality of interactions with our citizens?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Chairman, Sir, the Smart Nation initiative was first announced by Prime Minister Lee in 2014.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It aims to make Singapore into an outstanding city where people live, work and play in an innovation-rich environment.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Building a Smart Nation requires a concerted national effort which comprises three pillars: digital Government, digital economy and digital society.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the central coordinating agency for e-Government services, the Smart Nation and Digital Government Group has implemented a number of online services to benefit both businesses and our people.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These include services pertaining to CPF services, parking, libraries and SkillsFuture.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the town level, I wish to share some initiatives undertaken by the People's Action Party (PAP) Town Councils to support Smart Nation initiatives and to seek support from the Government to expedite the implementation of Smart Town technologies and features to benefit three million HDB residents.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the years, the PAP Town Councils have developed and implemented various information technology (IT) and digital solutions to better serve our residents.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These include, first, the computerisation of our financial system known as the Town Council Management System (TCMS) which integrates our system with those of various Government agencies, banks and service providers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, the computerisation and digitisation of our Complaint Management System called the Integrated Estate Management System (IEMS) which collects feedback from residents and stakeholders for maintenance and improvement purposes.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To support this objective, we have also developed the iTown mobile application for residents to provide feedback on Town Council matters and a dashboard management system for IEMS.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, Holland-Bukit Panjang Town Council has embarked on a number of Smart Town initiatives to improve township management services for residents.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have developed a Smart Barrier-Free Access (BFA) application to enable users of personal mobility aids to navigate BFA routes and facilities in Bukit Panjang Town.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are also exploring other smart town features, such as smart locks, for roof access, e-procurement and payment, and sensors for improving lift performance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In fact, some jurisdictions, like San Francisco, have banned such smart technologies, other than seriously looking at how best to balance and manage the privacy concerns that accompany such platforms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the flipside, in light of manpower constraints and the prospect for effective monitoring and deterrence – the public's difficult relationship with some users of PMDs come to mind – the benefits of these new technologies are readily apparent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We have also read about rogue public officers, including Police officers, illegally accessing Government information in our newspapers in the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: While these numbers are very small, new technologies and smart platforms host so much more information and data of a personal nature that people can lose confidence and trust in public service very quickly should an untoward incident occur.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There is also the attendant risk of cybersecurity incidents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It has been two-and-a-half years since the Prime Minister announced details on the Smart Nation digital platform at the 2017 National Day Rally.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What have been the results of the pilot so far, not just from the technical data acquisition perspective but the processing, handling and control perspective?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is it the PMO's view that our data protection laws are fit for purpose to accommodate the advent of these new technologies which have significant repercussions on individual privacy?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) has transformed the way we collect, store and use data.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has heralded in an era characterised by the blurring of digital and physical boundaries, and the growing use of new technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, robotics, 3D printing and the Internet of Things (IoT).

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the push for a Smart Nation, the Singapore Government, through the Government Technology Agency (GovTech), has introduced various initiatives to streamline the provision of Government services online and through digital platforms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we have been making steady progress towards realising the vision of a Smart Nation Singapore, the complexity and amount of data that the Government has to manage has also increased correspondingly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In recent years, we have seen several instances where Government data was compromised.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2019 alone, two high-profile breaches surfaced where medical data of individuals were leaked online.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government provide an update on the action plan to implement the recommendations, and how is the Government ensuring robust data security, even as it uses data more extensively?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's Government is leading by example in making Singapore a Smart Nation, with more and more Government agencies providing services online and more and more services being automated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One is able to apply for passports online and collect with minimal fuss.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Clearing immigration is also automated for Singaporeans at the various checkpoints, making clearance a breeze.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Filling out taxes is a painful process in many places, but, here, for most people, it is just a few clicks on an online system and our tax form for the year is done.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a National Serviceman (NSman), a reservist, it has become increasingly easy to get things done, including going for medical check-ups, taking the Individual Physical Proficiency Test (IPPT) and even acknowledging call-ups.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, as service users, life for us has become very easy, so much so that we may even take it for granted.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For this speech, for example, I am actually using my smartphone, rather than the paper I normally use.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, we are all trying to go smart.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But, of course, we recognise this requires significant state resources.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What is the Government doing to build up public sector capabilities in harnessing digitalisation?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And how can it ensure that it is able to attract enough engineers and people of the right calibre to develop these systems?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chairman, I am a heavy user of technology.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And when I started on a technology project, I created a first layer of programming and algorithm where the machines started to learn.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With more data collected, more and more, the machine gets smarter and it could make intelligent decisions or informed decisions for me.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As it goes on, I realise that some of my staff actually were being replaced for the role that they played but they could co-exist with the technology itself, and I realise that that is AI.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: AI was extremely helpful for the companies that I run.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The staff themselves found that they could co-exist and become more productive and more clever in making the decisions.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am excited about the national AI project and I hope that the national AI project is not just internally focused, but externally focused as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As long as it enables and strengthens companies and individuals and helps Singaporeans in their daily lives, I think this AI Project will be very exciting instead of replacing jobs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Mr Chairman, businesses are often faced with processes that require approvals from multiple Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: This is time-consuming and expensive for businesses when they have to make physical visits to different agencies, provide similar information repeatedly on separate application forms and track the status of applications on different agency portals.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: It could become frustrating when business owners uncover additional regulatory requirements that they were unaware of, resulting in delays to their application process.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Currently, GovTech has launched the GoBusiness Licensing Portal and the Business Grants Portal.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Can the Minister advise if are there other touchpoints with businesses that will be streamlined?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There has been tremendous effort to implement measures to realise our aspirations of a digital economy, Government and society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the Government presses on, what new Smart Nation initiatives are there to deliver more personalised and inclusive services to citizens of all ages and of all backgrounds?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
